enrichment.short_title: Mowlem v Avon coroner: unlawful inquest wording and post-verdict comments
key_facts: Mowlem Plc sought judicial review of an inquest verdict into the death of carpenter Mr Cox, injured at the Bath Spa restoration site on 23 May 2003.
Paragraph 3 of the inquisition unlawfully recorded that he 'fell from a ladder at work' after staff typed disputed facts before the jury retired.
Neither Mowlem nor the coroner wanted a fresh inquest; the deceased's widow opposed one.
The coroner also made post-verdict comments about ladder risk assessments and accident-book completion in breach of Coroners Rules 1986 Rule 36.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of parts of a coroner's inquest verdict and of comments made after the jury's delivery.
enrichment.outcome: Court substituted 'he stumbled, tripped and/or fall at work' for the unlawful wording; declared the coroner's post-verdict comments unlawful and of no effect; coroner ordered to pay 100% of Mowlem's costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: On judicial review of inquisitions the court has a residual power under CPR 54.19(3) to substitute wording where the jury's determination cannot be identified but a neutral form covering all reasonable hypotheses would not misstate their verdict; coroners must not express opinions outside Rule 36(1) matters.
legal_issues: Whether the court could substitute words in an inquisition rather than order a fresh inquest
What wording accurately reflected the jury's determination on how the fatal injury occurred
Whether the coroner's post-verdict comments breached Rule 36(2)
From what date the coroner should be liable for the claimant's costs

enrichment.short_title: Campden Hill v Chakrani: forged loan and solicitor fraud at Tanners Hill
key_facts: Campden Hill Ltd lent £500,000 secured on 120 Tanners Hill after documents apparently signed by Mr Chakrani were provided through Mrs Karim of Karim Solicitors.
The judge found Mr Chakrani did not authorise the transaction and Mrs Karim forged his signature on the loan documentation.
Mrs Karim disbursed about £290,000 to accounts controlled by Mr Chakrani from the firm's client account.
The Karim defendants conceded liability for £500,000 if forgery was proved; facility fee and restitution/tracing against Mr Chakrani remained in issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claims for repayment, deceit, breach of warranty of authority, knowing receipt and restitution following a freezing order.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment confirms forgery and Karim defendants' liability for £500,000 with interest; facility fee damages discounted by 20%; tracing analysis proceeds but recorded text ends before final orders on all defendants.
enrichment.ratio: Where a solicitor forges a borrower's signature, she is liable in deceit and for breach of warranty of authority; a 40% six-month facility fee may be extortionate even on a secured loan; equitable tracing through a solicitors' client account is constrained by Clayton's case where claimant funds are exhausted before later payments.

Measure of damages for breach of warranty of authority including the £200,000 facility fee
Whether section 2 LP(MP)A 1989 or section 137 CCA 1974 barred enforcement of the facility fee

enrichment.short_title: Norris v SoS: Tunstall bypass CPO and exchange open space
key_facts: Mr Norris challenged the Secretary of State's October 2004 decision to make operative a compulsory purchase order for the Tunstall Northern By-pass.
A Joint Committee amendment required an additional 5.4 hectares of Clanway Farm open space beyond plots 6–9.
The Secretary of State accepted the council's Option B Phase 1 proposal with landscaped footpath links rather than land adjacent to the Greenway.
Norris argued the Secretary of State took irrelevant housing-viability considerations and failed to verify the bypass planning permission remained extant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 (not judicial review) challenging the operative CPO decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all three grounds: rationality challenge, bypass planning permission challenge and consultation challenge all failed.
enrichment.ratio: When comparing exchange-land proposals under Article 3A, the Secretary of State may lawfully consider deliverability, development potential and cost; he was not obliged to investigate the bypass planning permission before making the CPO operative where no party had raised lapse and criterion (iv) concerned open-space agreements only.
legal_issues: Whether housing viability and compulsory purchase cost were irrelevant to assessing additional open space
Whether the Secretary of State had to satisfy himself the bypass planning permission remained valid
Whether petitioners should have been consulted on planning permission status
Whether March 2002 works lawfully commenced the permitted development

enrichment.short_title: Azam v HPC: suspension after in-absence misconduct hearing
key_facts: Mr Azam, a registered biomedical scientist, was convicted of common assault and criminal damage and damaged NHS Trust property.
His HPC Conduct and Competence Committee refused a last-minute email adjournment and proceeded in his absence.
The panel found fitness to practise impaired by violence and imposed a six-month suspension with interim suspension pending appeal.
Because of Regulation 29(11), the suspension period had not started until the appeal was determined.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court against HPC suspension order following an in-absence fitness-to-practise hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both grounds; court encouraged Azam to apply under Regulation 30 for review of suspension; costs contribution assessed at £5,000.
enrichment.ratio: A disciplinary panel may refuse a same-day adjournment request where witnesses are present and the applicant does not deny the allegations; sentence falls for appellate interference only if outside the range of reasonable responses, especially where fellow professionals assess impact on public confidence.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to adjourn rendered the hearing unjust
Whether six months' suspension was unduly severe for a first disciplinary offence
Effect of interim suspension and Regulation 29(11) on timing of penalty
Appropriate costs order against a publicly funded regulator
linked_authorities: Newfield v The Law Society [2005] EWHC 765 (Admin)

enrichment.short_title: Equitas v Wave City: declarations on profit commission tort threat
key_facts: Wave City and related shipowners threatened to sue Equitas and Lloyd's syndicates over Hellenic war-risk reinsurance profit commission arrangements linked to the 1991 sinking of Demetra Beauty.
Equitas and ERL sought negative declarations after Greek lawyers indicated an impending claim that profit commission induced Hellenic to reject valid claims.
Defendants did not acknowledge service despite repeated warnings and proper service in Greece, Cyprus and Liberia.
Long history of acrimonious Greek litigation between the shipowners and Hellenic preceded the threatened English claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application for default declaratory judgment and costs after defendants failed to acknowledge service.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted that Equitas and underwriters were not liable on the threatened tort theories; defendants ordered to pay £42,765 costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5(3) Brussels Regulation permits a domiciled defendant's victim to sue in England for a declaration that no tort was committed where the harmful event occurred in London; profit commission clauses do not induce breach of underlying insurance without intention and knowledge, and no such tort was established on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the court had jurisdiction under Article 5(3) for negative declarations
Whether profit commission in reinsurance could constitute inducing breach of insurance contract
Whether declaratory relief was appropriate against non-participating defendants
Limitation and membership timing for Robin and Leoninus expulsion claims

enrichment.short_title: HFEA v Amicus: lawfulness of storing Evans embryos pending ECtHR
key_facts: Following Evans v Amicus in the Court of Appeal, Mr Johnston withdrew consent to storage of embryos created with Ms Evans at the Bath Assisted Conception Clinic.
Continued storage breached licence conditions and potentially section 41 HFE Act, but the ECtHR issued a Rule 39 indication to preserve embryos pending Strasbourg proceedings.
HFEA and the clinic sought declarations that regulatory forbearance and the DPP's non-prosecution stance were lawful.
Parties consented to first two declarations; third legitimate-expectation declaration was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for declaratory relief on lawfulness of HFEA non-enforcement and DPP prosecution policy while embryos remain stored.
enrichment.outcome: Court granted amended first and second declarations; declined third declaration on substantive legitimate expectation as a matter of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: HFEA may lawfully exercise its section 18 discretion not to revoke a licence where enforcement would conflict with the UK's Article 34 ECHR obligations; the DPP may publish policy guidance consistent with Pretty v DPP without granting immunity from prosecution for future offences.
legal_issues: Whether HFEA could refrain from licence enforcement pending ECtHR proceedings
Whether the DPP's public interest indication on section 41 prosecutions was lawful
Whether the clinic had a substantive legitimate expectation against enforcement or prosecution
Whether domestic courts could hold the ring pending Strasbourg determination

enrichment.short_title: Paulin: seven-year disqualification for Crown debt and asset hive-off
key_facts: Mr Paulin acquired Premier Screw from Tomkins via Croftacre and, while Crown debts rose by £540,362, paid £2.8m to other creditors.
On 26 October 2000 he caused the company to sell its business to group companies for set-off against debts not reflected in the accounts.
The Registrar found unfitness for trading to Crown detriment and a preferential transaction leaving the Revenue an empty shell.
Paulin sought late evidence after a reserved judgment and appealed both the refusal to admit it and the seven-year disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to a High Court judge against Registrar's disqualification order and refusal of permission to adduce post-trial evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; seven-year disqualification upheld; no permission required for appeal from Registrar under insolvency practice direction.
enrichment.ratio: Non-payment of Crown debts pursuant to a director's instruction and a pre-insolvency hive-off of assets to connected companies warrant disqualification; late evidence seeking a retrial after reserved judgment requires strong reasons and will be refused where it merely replugs gaps in an unsuccessful defence.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal a section 6 disqualification order is required
Whether the Registrar should have admitted further evidence after trial
Whether Crown debt non-payment and October 2000 sale rendered Paulin unfit
Whether seven years fell within the appropriate disqualification bracket

enrichment.short_title: PMS v NE Lincolnshire: £1 stationery set classified as toy
key_facts: A 12-year-old bought an 'A Plus Office Stationery Set' containing pens, stapler, scissors and a craft knife from a £1 shop.
Trading Standards prosecuted PMS (supplier) and the retailer after the set lacked child-safe pen caps and knife warnings.
Justices found the miniaturised, brightly coloured set was targeted at under-14s with play value despite office branding.
The set was displayed near children's colouring books and bore a CE mark styled like the toy safety mark.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' convictions under the Toys (Safety) Regulations 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions upheld; case remitted for sentence; respondents' costs assessed at £4,300.
enrichment.ratio: A product is a 'toy' if objectively designed or clearly intended for play by children under 14, assessed from targeting factors such as size, price, display and limited adult utility; inclusion of a craft knife unlawful for under-16s does not negate toy status when viewed in the round.
legal_issues: Whether manufacturers' subjective intent precluded a toy finding
Whether the CE mark and shop positioning were admissible indicia
Whether craft-knife inclusion made toy classification impossible
Whether expert evidence should have dictated the justices' conclusion

enrichment.short_title: Aegis v Revenue: costs of discontinued s.320 judicial review
key_facts: Aegis issued a Chancery GLO claim for FII/franked investment income tax restitution and also applied to judicial review section 320 Finance Act 2004.
Section 320 reversed limitation advantages from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and was listed as GLO issue (Q).
Dorsey & Whitney invoked the judicial review pre-action protocol but the Revenue did not reply for nearly two months.
The judicial review claim was transferred to the Chancery Division and discontinued; validity of s.320 to be litigated under issue (Q).

enrichment.outcome: Aegis ordered to pay 85% of the Revenue's assessed procedural costs of the discontinued judicial review; permission would have been refused had the claim continued.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review was a misconceived vehicle where GLO issue (Q) provided an adequate Chancery remedy and s.320(3) did not preclude raising invalidity in those proceedings; Revenue breach of the pre-action protocol justified only a 15% costs reduction.

enrichment.short_title: Sheppard twins: appeal against claimants' costs cap order
key_facts: Twins Toby and Louisa Sheppard claim negligent management of hydrocephalus shunts caused additional brain damage, stroke and lifelong dependency.
Claimants estimate total costs over £515,000 against defendants' estimate of about £162,000; damages claimed exceed £5 million combined.
Master Ungley imposed a costs cap on claimants' costs with levels to be fixed by a Costs Judge after wide estimate disparities.
The case has a long history, eleven experts approved, and substantial costs already incurred over many years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Master Ungley's costs-capping order under CPR 52.11 in ongoing clinical negligence litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; costs cap in principle upheld and referral to Costs Judge for level regarded as appropriate prospective control.
enrichment.ratio: Where publicly funded clinical negligence litigation shows a real risk of unreasonable or disproportionate future costs that post-trial assessment may not effectively control, the court may impose a prospective costs cap or budget as part of active case management under the CPR overriding objective.
legal_issues: Whether Master Ungley erred in imposing a costs cap on the claimants
Whether there was a real risk of disproportionate or unreasonable costs
Whether conventional case management and detailed assessment sufficed
Appropriate test following Smart v East Cheshire and Leigh v Michelin
